hook: Down to 22 birds, biologists captured every last one. It worked.

story.text: A condor crosses the canyon without a single wingbeat: nine and a half feet of black wing, white triangles beneath, a bare head the color of sunrise.
It rides thermals to fifteen thousand feet and covers a hundred miles or more in a day, searching for the dead.
Carrion is its entire livelihood — anything already dead, from mice to beached whales.
By 1982, twenty-two California condors existed on Earth.
So biologists made a desperate gamble: on April 19, 1987, the last wild bird was caught, and the entire species went into captive breeding.
Five years later, condors returned to the California sky; Arizona followed in 1996.
The threat that remains is invisible: a lead bullet shatters into fragments inside a carcass, and the scavenger swallows the poison with the meal.
Every wild condor wears a numbered tag, and biologists trap each one yearly to test its blood for lead.
To witness the condor is to see extinction refused: 596 birds now, more than half of them flying free.
The recovery holds through choices — copper bullets instead of lead, trash packed out of condor country, and cliffs kept wild.

Status uses the federal ESA listing wording (fws.gov blocks automated verification; NPS states the 1967 listing). Region circles cover release-flock ranges, not nest sites.

stats.diet: Carrion only — mice to beached whales

reproduction.text: A single egg every other year, incubated by both parents for eight weeks. The chick fledges at five to six months, matures around six years, and most condors mate for life — one of the slowest rhythms of any bird.

insight.text: A condor can climb to fifteen thousand feet almost without flapping, riding columns of sun-warmed air at up to 55 miles per hour.

programs.title: Free non-lead ammunition
programs.summary: Has given central-California hunters and ranchers over 19,000 free boxes of non-lead ammunition since 2012, removing lead from the condor's food supply at its source.

programs.title: Condor restoration
programs.summary: Breeds condors and has released them at Vermilion Cliffs since 1996 — more than a hundred now fly free over the Grand Canyon region.
